articles.title: Lucky Bamboo: Best Placement for Money, Career and Family Luck This October
articles.summary: Lucky bamboo might be the easiest \"good luck\" plant you'll ever own.
articles.body: Lucky bamboo might be the easiest "good luck" plant you'll ever own. It barely needs soil, survives low light and costs less than a pumpkin spice latte at most grocery stores.But in feng shui, where you put it matters more than how pretty it looks. A stalk tucked behind the TV doesn't do much. The right corner, though? That can change how a room feels.Fun fact first. Lucky bamboo isn't actually bamboo. It's a type of dracaena. The feng shui meaning stays the same either way.Why October Is a Good Time to Add One2026 is the Year of the Fire Horse. Fire energy is fast and exciting, though it can leave homes feeling restless.Bamboo belongs to the wood element, which feeds steady growth. And the water it sits in adds calm. So a healthy lucky bamboo plant brings a little balance into a fiery year. With fall cleaning already underway in many homes, it's a natural time to bring one in.For Money: The Wealth CornerStand at your front door facing inside. The far left corner of your home, or of any single room, is known as the wealth area in Western feng shui.Place your lucky bamboo there. A home office desk works especially well, since that's where many people handle bills and budgets.If you follow the compass method instead, look for the southeast part of your home. Both approaches are common, so pick the one that makes sense to you.Choose a plant with five, six or eight stalks for wealth. Tie a red or gold ribbon around them. In Chinese tradition, both colours are linked with prosperity.For Career: Near the Entrance or Your DeskIn Western feng shui, the career area sits at the front centre of a home, near the main door. Compass-based feng shui puts it in the north.A small arrangement on an entry table helps "welcome" new opportunities. Working from home? Then set it on the left side of your desk, within your line of sight. Seeing something green and growing during a long workday does wonders for focus.Three stalks are a popular choice here, since the number is tied to happiness and good fortune.For Family: The Middle Left WallFamily harmony connects with the middle section of the left wall when you stand at the front door. The compass equivalent is east.The living room is ideal, since that's where the family gathers. A tall bamboo arrangement on a side table or bookshelf works well. Add family photos close by to strengthen the intention.Many people choose nine stalks for family luck, because nine stands for completeness and long life in Chinese tradition.Stalk Numbers to KnowTwo stalks represent love and partnership. Seven is often linked with health. Larger counts like 21 are sometimes gifted as powerful blessings for big milestones.But avoid four. In Chinese, the word for four sounds a lot like the word for death, so it's considered unlucky.Keep It HealthyA yellowing plant sends the opposite message of luck. So care matters.Use filtered or distilled water if your tap water is heavily treated, since chlorine and fluoride can brown the leaves. Change the water every week or two. Keep it out of harsh direct sunlight, which burns the leaves quickly.One more thing. Lucky bamboo is toxic to cats and dogs. If you have pets that like to chew plants, place it on a high shelf out of reach.Spots to SkipBathrooms drain energy in feng shui, so keep bamboo out of them unless it's purely decorative. Also avoid placing it right next to a trash can or in a dark, cluttered corner.And if a stalk dies, remove it promptly. Replace it so the total number still carries a good meaning.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: From vehicle seizure to licence suspension: What happens if you don’t pay traffic challans?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ignoring traffic challans could soon mean more than just an unpaid fine.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ignoring traffic challans could soon mean more than just an unpaid fine. The Supreme Court has directed states and Union territories to take stringent action against vehicles with pending e-challans, including impounding them and blocking several online services until the dues are cleared.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan said simply issuing e-challans was not enough, noting that nearly 47% of challans issued across the country remain unpaid.The court directed authorities to carry out random checks and impound vehicles if they are found to have outstanding e-challans.RC, fitness, PUC services may be blockedThe Supreme Court said online services for vehicles with unpaid traffic fines should be frozen. Authorities should bar renewal of registration certificates (RCs), issuance of duplicate RCs and requests to update the owner's address until pending fines are cleared.The court also directed authorities to deny fitness certificates to such vehicles and blacklist them on the Parivahan portal.The restrictions could also affect vehicle ownership transfers. The court said authorities should block the transfer of ownership of vehicles with outstanding challans, potentially preventing owners from selling them.Most significantly, the bench directed that no centre should be permitted to issue a pollution under control (PUC) certificate for vehicles with pending traffic fines.Driving licence action for multiple violationsThe Supreme Court also called for action against repeat offenders. For multiple traffic violations, authorities should stop renewal of the driving licence and take steps to suspend licences that are currently valid, the bench said.“Let there be random checking of vehicles, and if it is found that the e-challan issued has not been abided or honoured, necessary steps shall be taken to impound the vehicle itself,” the court said.Pulling up authorities for failing to recover pending fines, the bench said issuing lakhs of e-challans was not enough and questioned what was being done to actually recover the money.Rs 49,194 crore in challans pending recoveryThe court was informed that states and UTs have around Rs 49,194 crore to recover from e-challans issued over a period of time. Of this, around Rs 26,175 crore has been recovered, leaving a substantial amount still outstanding.The bench said authorities needed to work at the ground level and take into account the realities of enforcement.“We want to convey something to states/UTs/authorities in a plain and simple manner. It is not just sufficient to keep issuing e-challans to the person who is alleged to have violated the provisions of the law,” the court said.The case has been before the Supreme Court for nearly 14 years, after the writ petition was filed in 2012. The court said it had issued several directions over the years for effective implementation of the Motor Vehicles Act and Central Motor Vehicles Rules.It warned that if its directions continued to remain only on paper, the court could take “stern action” against the authorities.What can happen if traffic challans remain unpaid?Vehicle can be impounded during random checks.RC renewal can be blocked.Duplicate RC issuance can be stopped.Owner-address updates can be denied.Fitness certificate can be withheld.Vehicle can be blacklisted on Parivahan.Ownership transfer can be blocked, making it difficult to sell the vehicle.Driving licence renewal can be stopped in cases involving multiple violations.Existing driving licence can be suspended.PUC certificate can be denied.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to hold a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at Mumbai’s
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to hold a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park today, with founder Abhijeet Dipke making a fresh appeal to people to join the protest.In a new video, Dipke was seen posing with an auto driver as the two urged commuters and residents to gather at the protest venue. "Chala chala shivaji park.. shivaji park… shivaji park…," the caption reads.The auto driver in the video can be heard saying 'Shivaji Park 4 baje'.The CJP has announced a “Jail Bharo Andolan” against Kumar at Shivaji Park at 4pm, Gate No. 6, demanding Kumar’s resignation over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Protest planned across citiesMassive protests are planned in Delhi and Mumbai today, with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) set to launch its nationwide agitation from Mumbai’s Shivaji Park, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), All India Students’ Association (AISA), National Students’ Union of India (NSUI) and Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have announced a separate demonstration at Jantar Mantar in Delhi.The CJP has said its agitation will be expanded to other parts of the country.“Appointment of CEC should be transparent; there should be involvement of civil society,” Dipke said in Mumbai.Police deny permission in Delhi, MumbaiPolice in both Delhi and Mumbai have denied permission for the proposed protests. In Delhi, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) are in force across the New Delhi district, restricting public meetings or assemblies of five or more people, processions, demonstrations, picketing and dharnas without prior written permission.Delhi DCP said that the restrictions have been imposed to ensure public safety, maintain public order and facilitate smooth traffic movement.In Mumbai, police have also denied permission for the proposed gathering at Shivaji Park. Police said they were not authorised to permit such a gathering there in view of a 2013 Bombay High Court order and described the area as a silence zone.Meanwhile, multi-layer barricades have been put up on roads leading to Jantar Mantar, including Tolstoy Marg, Janpath Road and Sansad Marg. The Delhi Metro has also closed entry and exit at 11 stations, including Rajiv Chowk, Central Secretariat, Janpath, Patel Chowk, Seva Teerth, Mandi House, Lok Kalyan Marg, INA, Chawri Bazar, Ramakrishna Ashram Marg and New Delhi, until further notice.Why are protests being held against Gyanesh Kumar?The CJP and opposition parties have criticised Kumar over the SIR of electoral rolls and demanded his resignation.Their criticism intensified after it emerged that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months to certain decisions and orders, some of which they said were issued without their knowledge.The Election Commission later clarified that the three-member commission had taken all decisions, including those relating to the SIR, unanimously.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: He never married or had children; after his death, his estate began funding engineering students at NC State, where he once studied
articles.summary: Guy Burke never married and had no children, but his legacy has continued to teach students at the university where he once struggled to afford his
articles.body: Guy Burke never married and had no children, but his legacy has continued to teach students at the university where he once struggled to afford his education. His connection with NC State began in 1953, when his interest in aircraft led him to study mechanical and aeronautical engineering. His path to graduation was interrupted several times after his father’s death forced him to leave college to earn money for tuition. Military service caused another break. Burke finally graduated in 1962 and spent three decades as a civilian employee of the US Navy. After his death in 2019, the estate gift he had arranged decades earlier became a scholarship supporting engineering students.Burke’s college journey took him from engineering classes to drafting workBurke grew up in Taylorsville, North Carolina, as the eldest of four siblings. His brothers remembered him as a capable student who also enjoyed baseball. In 1953, his interest in aeroplanes led him towards engineering at NC State.The early part of university life was relatively ordinary. He lived in Owen Hall, took part in ROTC, which was compulsory at the time, and worked through his engineering courses. But the subject was difficult for him. He was apparently more naturally comfortable with writing and drawing than some of the technical demands of the degree. Then, in May 1955, the family lost its father, Walton.The financial consequences changed Burke’s education. His mother could cover the family’s basic needs, but there was little left for university fees and living costs. Burke began moving in and out of college, working until he had saved enough to return.As reported by NC State University, at one point, he stayed at a relative’s hunting lodge and worked as a draftsman designing bridges for the state highway department. His university education became something he pursued between periods of employment rather than in one uninterrupted stretch.Burke returned to NC State after two years teaching soldiers at Fort SillBurke’s return to college did not mean his path was settled. In 1959, he was drafted into the US Army and spent two years at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, where he worked as an artillery instructor. He also played softball on the base. Teaching suited him, according to his family, and the experience became another part of a life in which education and work repeatedly overlapped.After completing his service, Burke returned to NC State. He finally finished his remaining courses in the summer of 1962. His brother David later described the experience as a story of determination to become an engineer at NC State.Three decades working for the US NavyBurke subsequently spent about 30 years as a civilian employee of the US Navy. His engineering background placed him in work connected with early military uses of GPS, at a time when the technology was still far removed from the consumer devices that would eventually make satellite navigation familiar to the public. Away from work, he had a strong interest in sport and collecting memorabilia. He held season tickets for the NFL's Washington Commanders and was a regular at games.Later in life, after retiring to Cary, North Carolina, Burke helped care for his sister Janice. He continued attending NC State sporting events and followed the Carolina Hurricanes. Burke was a careful investor and kept money in a range of mutual funds. His family described him as disciplined with his finances rather than someone who spent lavishly.Burke planned his NC State gift more than two decades before his deathBurke contacted NC State's College of Engineering in 1997 to ask about making a contribution. He did not immediately settle on what form that gift should take. After considering his options for several months, he decided to leave part of his estate to the university through his will.The choice of destination was closely connected to his own experience. He wanted the money to support engineering students, with scholarships taking both academic merit and financial need into account. That decision was made more than two decades before his death.Burke died on 22 March 2019, aged with no children to inherit the estate. His brother David, who served as executor, later worked with NC State's Office of Gift Planning to carry out the wishes set out in Burke's will. The resulting Burke Endowment began supporting students in 2020.Scholarships ease financial pressure for engineering studentsReportedly, for the 2025-26 academic year, 15 students from different class years received scholarships supported by the endowment. Some have worked throughout university to cover tuition and housing, while others have worried about taking on student debt or being able to study full-time.Angela Sarahi Hernandez, a member of the class of 2028, said, “The Burke Endowment has allowed me to attend NC State as a fulltime student rather than being a part-time student. Spending more time on campus has enabled me to focus on my academics and pursue undergraduate research.”For J. Blake Patterson, from the class of 2027 described, “The Burke Endowment has allowed me to pursue my degree without the burden of student loan debt, limiting my stress and making my NC State experience more enjoyable.”How a $500 act of support shaped the Burke family legacyAfter Walton Burke died, the local Lions Club, where his father had been a member, lent Guy $500 to help him remain in education. He could repay the money when he was able.When Guy eventually had enough money to settle the debt, the club did something unexpected. Rather than taking the repayment, members told him to give the money to his sister so that she could use it for her own education. The same arrangement was then extended to Gerald. That single $500 loan therefore helped three Burke siblings through school. Gerald eventually repaid the money to a club treasurer who no longer remembered the original loan and had no record of it.Burke’s legacy now supports students facing financial challengesGuy Burke's life did not follow the conventional pattern of leaving a family home, business or fortune to children. He was an unmarried man without children, remembered by his relatives for his engineering career, sporting interests, collecting and careful approach to money.His estate took on a different role. The provision he made in 1997 eventually became an endowment supporting students at the university where he had once struggled to pay for his own education. It has continued awarding scholarships each year since 2020.For his family, the connection between Burke's own circumstances and the students now receiving the money is difficult to miss. He knew what it meant to interrupt an education because of finances. He also knew what a modest helping hand could do, having benefited from the $500 loan given to his family.Decades after he first approached NC State about making a gift, the money he set aside is now being used by students working towards the same kind of qualification he once had to fight to complete.You use AI every day. articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has called the H-1B visa programme “completely broken” and said he would support scrapping it, accusing companies of using the
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has called the H-1B visa programme “completely broken” and said he would support scrapping it, accusing companies of using the system to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees.In a video shared on X, Vance said the programme had been “totally taken advantage of” by technology companies, accounting firms and other businesses. He distinguished between hiring highly skilled foreign professionals and using H-1B visas to reduce labour costs.“If you’re going to bring in an accountant making $45,000 a year to replace an accountant who is an American making $60,000 a year, that’s not you using the programme to bring in a genius,” Vance said.“That’s you destroying American jobs and defrauding the American people,” he added.Vance defends $100,000 H-1B feeVance also defended the Trump administration’s controversial $100,000 payment requirement for certain H-1B petitions involving workers outside the US. The White House introduced the measure in September 2025 and extended it for another year in September 2026.Vance said the payment was intended to discourage companies from using the programme to hire cheaper foreign labour.“If you’re just trying to replace an American accountant with a cheaper foreign accountant, then you’re not going to pay $100,000,” he said.However, the fee is currently blocked following a federal court ruling. A second US district judge in California blocked enforcement of the $100,000 fee, finding that the administration had not followed the required rulemaking procedures.Vance’s remarks come as the Trump administration pursues broader changes to the H-1B system. A September 18 executive order directs the Departments of State, Labour and Homeland Security to consider whether an employer has recently laid off, or plans to lay off, similarly situated US workers while reviewing H-1B applications. It also directs the Labour Department to review previously filed labour-condition applications for possible violations.The administration has separately introduced a weighted H-1B selection system that gives greater weight to higher-paid positions.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Jack Johnson's foundation bought neglected farmland in Hawaii; six years later, it reported over 40,000 pounds of produce harvested and more than 2,200 students welcomed on field trips
articles.summary: In 2019, musician Jack Johnson’s Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation acquired neglected farmland on Oʻahu with a plan to turn it into a place for education, food
articles.body: In 2019, musician Jack Johnson’s Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation acquired neglected farmland on Oʻahu with a plan to turn it into a place for education, food production and community involvement. Six years later, the Kōkua Learning Farm had reported harvesting more than 40,000 pounds of produce and welcoming over 2,200 students on educational field trips. The figures were included in a document submitted to the City and County of Honolulu, while the foundation’s Kōkua Learning Farm website describes the site’s wider work in farming, composting, agroforestry and food education. What began as a neglected agricultural property has gradually become a working classroom where children, teachers, volunteers and young farmers can learn how food is grown.From neglected land to a working farmThe Kōkua Learning Farm was created on land that had not been fully used for many years. Rather than treating the property simply as a place to grow crops, the foundation imagined a broader community resource that could connect people with Hawaiʻi’s food systems.The farm’s work reflects the Kōkua Hawaiʻi Foundation’s focus on environmental education and sustainable living. Its programmes encourage students to understand where food comes from, how soil is maintained and why healthy ecosystems are important to farms and communities.Turning neglected land into productive farmland required more than planting seeds. The property needed preparation, infrastructure, soil care and a long-term plan for managing water, crops, pathways and educational spaces. The gradual transformation allowed the organisation to build the farm around practical learning instead of creating a purely decorative garden.By the sixth year, the site had become a functioning agricultural operation. More than 40,000 pounds of produce had been harvested, showing how much food can emerge when land is restored with consistent care and community support.A place where students learn by doingOne of the farm’s most important roles is educational. More than 2,200 students had visited the property on field trips during the six years covered in the city document.The visits are designed to help students experience the food system directly. Instead of learning only from textbooks or classroom diagrams, children can see crops growing, examine soil, observe insects and discuss what happens to food scraps after meals.The foundation says field trips can include lessons on food production, compost, agroforestry and pollinators. Activities are adapted according to the age of the students, the size of the group and what is happening on the farm during the visit.That flexibility is important because farming is seasonal. A group visiting during planting will have a different experience from one arriving during harvest. Students may encounter seedlings, mature crops, composting projects, fruit trees or pollinator habitats, depending on the time of year.Hawaiian knowledge and ecological learningThe farm’s educational approach is also connected to Hawaiʻi’s relationship with the ʻāina, or land. The Kōkua Learning Farm website describes a Hawaiian Garden as the final piece of the farm’s development. The garden was designed through a collaborative process involving experts and community organisations.Such spaces can help students understand that agriculture is not only about producing food. It is also about caring for soil, water, plants, animals and the cultural knowledge connected to a place.The farm’s work includes agroforestry, a method that brings trees and crops together in a managed system. It also includes lessons about compost and pollinators, two parts of agriculture that are often overlooked when people focus only on the food found in markets.By bringing these subjects together, the farm gives visitors a more complete picture of how food is produced. A tomato or leafy green is not just the result of a seed and sunlight. It depends on soil health, water, pollinating insects, farm workers and careful management of the surrounding environment.Volunteers help keep the farm growingThe transformation of the property has also depended on public participation. The foundation hosts monthly community workdays, generally on the first Saturday of the month.Volunteers may help with mulching, weeding, collecting ʻōpala, or waste, working in the nursery, planting and harvesting. These tasks are ordinary parts of farm work, but they also give community members a direct role in maintaining the property.Private workdays are available for schools, businesses, churches, clubs, military groups and other organisations. These gatherings allow groups to work together outdoors while learning how much regular labour is needed to care for productive land.The farm also provides opportunities for individual volunteers during weekdays. This creates a connection between the property and the wider community, ensuring that the site is supported by more than a small staff.A training ground for young farmersThe Kōkua Learning Farm is not limited to younger children. It also runs a youth internship programme for students in grades nine through twelve.High school students from public schools, private schools and homeschool programmes can apply to become part of the cohort. Participants meet weekly and receive practical training as mahiʻai, or farmers.The programme covers agroecology, crop cultivation, fruit and vegetable production, soil health maintenance and culinary exploration. These sessions give teachers hands-on opportunities to explore lessons that can later be used with students.That approach allows the farm’s influence to extend beyond visitors. A teacher who learns about composting, soil health or food production can take those ideas back to a school and introduce them to a much larger group of children.The site also hosts community events, farm workdays and farm-to-table activities. These programmes help connect food production with cooking, culture and shared community experiences.A long-term vision for the landSix years after the foundation acquired the neglected farmland, the Kōkua Learning Farm had become an example of what long-term restoration can achieve. The property was producing food, receiving school groups and giving volunteers a place to work with the land.Its progress also shows that restoring farmland is not an overnight project. The results depend on repeated tasks such as planting, harvesting, mulching, composting, repairing infrastructure and teaching visitors how the system works.Jack Johnson’s connection to the foundation has helped bring public attention to the project, but the farm’s development has relied on educators, farmers, students, volunteers and community partners.
